claims.statement: Wang Shuo made his qi observations by reference to the vapours beside the sun.

claims.event: Wang Shuo's method of observing qi beside the sun (no date in the source unit).

claims.statement: Wei Xian of the Han compiled prognostications of the eight winds from the day after the La festival and the dawn of the first month.

claims.event: Wei Xian's compilation on the eight winds, done in the Han period (after the Han founding in 206 BC).

claims.statement: The Grand Historian's discourse: rulers since the first people have always reckoned by the sun, moon and stars; the Five Emperors and Three Dynasties clarified this; since Kings You and Li records diverged; Confucius recorded anomalies without the explanations.

claims.event: The Grand Historian's discourse on astronomy (no date in the source units).

claims.statement: The Grand Historian names the time of Kings You and Li as the point after which celestial records became ancient and divergent.

claims.event: Reign of King Li of Zhou (conventional dates; independently established, not from this passage).

claims.statement: The Grand Historian names the time of Kings You and Li as the point after which celestial records became ancient and divergent.

claims.event: Reign of King You of Zhou (conventional dates; independently established, not from this passage).

claims.statement: In discussing the Six Classics, Confucius recorded anomalies but did not write down their explanations.

claims.event: Confucius's lifetime (conventional dates; independently established, not from this passage).

claims.statement: Gaoxin is named as the time before which Zhong and Li transmitted the celestial numbers.

claims.event: Gaoxin named as a chronological marker in the list of transmitters (legendary; no date).

claims.statement: Zhong is listed by the Grand Historian among those who transmitted the celestial numbers, before Gaoxin.

claims.event: Zhong, a legendary transmitter before Gaoxin (no date).

claims.statement: Li is listed by the Grand Historian among those who transmitted the celestial numbers, before Gaoxin.

claims.event: Li, a legendary transmitter before Gaoxin (no date).

claims.statement: Xi is listed by the Grand Historian among those who transmitted the celestial numbers in the time of Tang and Yu.

claims.event: Xi, legendary astronomer of the Tang and Yu period (no date).

claims.statement: He is listed by the Grand Historian among those who transmitted the celestial numbers in the time of Tang and Yu.

claims.event: He, legendary astronomer of the Tang and Yu period (no date).

claims.statement: Kunwu is listed by the Grand Historian among those who transmitted the celestial numbers under the Xia.

claims.event: Kunwu, legendary astronomer of the Xia (no date).

claims.statement: Wu Xian is listed by the Grand Historian among those who transmitted the celestial numbers under Yin-Shang.

claims.event: Wu Xian, astronomer of Yin-Shang (no date given).

claims.statement: Shi Yi is listed by the Grand Historian among those who transmitted the celestial numbers at the Zhou court.

claims.event: Shi Yi served the Zhou court (after the Zhou conquest, conventionally 1046 BC).

claims.statement: Chang Hong is listed by the Grand Historian among those who transmitted the celestial numbers at the Zhou court.

claims.event: Chang Hong served the Zhou court (after the Zhou conquest, conventionally 1046 BC).

claims.statement: Ziwei is listed by the Grand Historian among those who transmitted the celestial numbers in Song.

claims.event: Ziwei of Song (no date in the source unit).

claims.statement: Pi Zao is listed by the Grand Historian among those who transmitted the celestial numbers in Zheng.

claims.event: Pi Zao of Zheng (no date in the source unit).

claims.statement: Gan Gong is listed by the Grand Historian among those who transmitted the celestial numbers in Qi; with Gao, Tang and Shi he discussed the books according to current affairs, and his five-planet method with Shi's recognised only Mars as retrograde.

claims.event: Gan, Tang, Gao and Shi wrote in the era when the seven states styled themselves kings (s0778).

claims.statement: Tang Mei is listed by the Grand Historian among those who transmitted the celestial numbers in Chu; with Gao, Gan and Shi he discussed the books according to current affairs.

claims.event: Tang Mei wrote in the era when the seven states styled themselves kings (s0778).

claims.statement: Yin Gao is listed by the Grand Historian among those who transmitted the celestial numbers in Zhao; with Tang, Gan and Shi he discussed the books according to current affairs.

claims.event: Yin Gao wrote in the era when the seven states styled themselves kings (s0778).

claims.statement: Shi Shen is listed by the Grand Historian among those who transmitted the celestial numbers in Wei; with Gao, Tang and Gan he discussed the books according to current affairs, and his five-planet method with Gan's recognised only Mars as retrograde.

claims.event: Shi Shen wrote in the era when the seven states styled themselves kings (s0778).

claims.statement: The Grand Historian surveyed ancient celestial changes and recent omens from the Spring and Autumn period to the Han campaigns.

claims.event: The Grand Historian's survey of ancient celestial changes (no date in the source unit).

claims.statement: Stars fell like rain in the time of Duke Xiang of Song.

claims.event: Reign of Duke Xiang of Song (conventional dates, independently established; the source gives none).

claims.statement: In the First Emperor's time comets appeared four times in fifteen years; afterwards Qin destroyed the six kings and annexed the central states.

claims.event: Reign of the First Emperor of Qin (conventional dates, independently established).

claims.statement: The Grand Historian says that since Chiyou there had never been such slaughter.

claims.event: Chiyou named as the legendary point of comparison for slaughter (no date).

claims.statement: Xiang Yu relieved Julu, the Wanshi star flowed west, and the eastern lords allied, buried the Qin troops and slaughtered Xianyang.

claims.event: Xiang Yu's relief of Julu (conventionally 207 BC; the source gives no year).

claims.statement: Tang Du is named as the Han authority on the stars.

claims.event: Tang Du practised the celestial numbers under the Han (after 206 BC).

claims.statement: Wang Shuo is named as the Han authority on qi.

claims.event: Wang Shuo practised qi observation under the Han (after 206 BC).

claims.statement: Wei Xian is named as the Han authority on divining the year.

claims.event: Wei Xian practised year divination under the Han (after 206 BC).

unresolvedReferences.description: The Grand Historian (太史公) is not otherwise identified here (Sima Qian or his father Sima Tan); kept as a title-only person.

Stars falling like rain is dated by the Spring and Autumn Annals to Duke Zhuang of Lu's 7th year (687 BC), not the time of Duke Xiang of Song (r. 650-637) as stated here; Duke Xiang's dates are conventional.
The Grand Historian (太史公) is not further identified (Sima Qian or Sima Tan).
